# Learning objectives and NICE Framework mapping

<!-- Generated by python -m ridge.learning_objectives --write from
     assets/learning-objectives-v1.json. Edit the fixture, not this file. -->

Operation Silent Ridge is a cooperative defensive exercise. This document
states what participants should be able to do afterwards, names the exercise
mechanism that produces each capability rather than describing the topic, and
records where that mechanism lives. It is written for the expanded
implementation: twenty IRIS tickets, each with four CTFd coached questions,
analysed with Wireshark, Autopsy, Wazuh, Cutter and a Linux file manager.
Participants reach the queue and the findings through IRIS, the questions and
the points through CTFd, and the shared desktop through Guacamole; the Wazuh
dashboard is opened in their own browser. Every claim below is rendered from
`assets/learning-objectives-v1.json` and checked against the tree it describes,
so this file cannot drift from the exercise. See also the [narrative
overview](narrative-overview.md).

The framework mapping below is unverified and says so. Everything else in this
document is derived from committed source and regenerated with `python -m
ridge.learning_objectives --write`.

## How learning is facilitated

1. Authentic, deterministic artifacts. `expanded/prepare.py` generates a
   purpose-built FAT16 image with a recoverable deleted cache entry, a valid
   DNS capture, a reconstructed syslog capture that matches the proxy export,
   the browser, authentication, server and coverage exports, and the historical
   replay. Stable source hashes replace conspicuous suspicious-record ranges,
   and the artifact verifier checks every released category.
2. Tool-mediated analysis. Each ticket names a tool and a starting selection:
   Wireshark with a display filter, Autopsy with the writable case copy and a
   named record, Wazuh with one of the two provisioned saved views and a named
   field filter, Cutter with a harmless static training binary, and the desktop
   file manager for a CSV or JSON comparison. Participants learn the tool by
   answering a specific, evidence-bounded question.
3. Coached, gated questions. Teams claim one IRIS ticket at a time and its four
   CTFd questions are answerable only by the owner. Hints and the full
   walkthrough are free. Each question states the rule the repository grades by
   - enter only the requested value, and case and outer whitespace are ignored
   - which is a narrower promise than a normalised answer and is what
   `expanded/author.py` actually implements. A correct answer earns one point,
   queues an authored finding for IRIS and persists globally; the last answer
   closes the ticket and unlocks authored follow-ups, which is what sequences
   the phases.
4. Durable shared findings with transactional receipts. Accepted answers queue
   IRIS findings and CTFd awards through durable outbox retries and
   application-side receipts. Relinquishing a ticket retains its answers and
   findings for the replacement owner. Live IRIS and cross-system outage
   acceptance remain gates; see `docs/expanded-validation.md`.
5. Machine-enforced limits on what may be claimed. `ridge/scenario_contract.py`
   refuses any participant-facing string containing a distinctive scored answer
   in `check_no_answers`, and refuses an exemption that is not already public
   in `check_public_terms`; `ridge/narrative_consistency.py` adds ten
   cross-surface guards; `ridge/network_map.py` requires every edge to declare
   observed or inferred provenance with a basis and a caveat. This document is
   held to the same rule.
6. A narrative with every ticket. Each authored ticket carries its phase,
   briefing, stake and handoff, so the room hears why a ticket matters before
   opening a tool. The [narrative overview](narrative-overview.md) describes
   how the two narrative contracts differ and which one is still undecided.
7. Optional breadcrumbs with no bonus. Seven optional traces are left across
   the evidence; none is scored, and a team that finds none has done the
   exercise correctly. The mapping is in `facilitator/breadcrumbs.md`.

| Surface | Where a participant reaches it | Narrative source |
|---|---|---|
| IRIS incident queue and findings | the shared `/silent-ridge` queue | narrative contract |
| CTFd questions, points and scoreboard | one award per accepted answer | authored questions |
| Guacamole shared desktop | the team desktop session | operational |
| Wazuh dashboard | opened in the participant's own browser | two saved views, no narrative |
| Evidence tree | `/evidence` read-only, `/originals` read-only | released and acquired artifacts |
| Event-day deck | 22 participant slides plus a 2-slide facilitator appendix | narrative contract |
| T01 network map | the question page, gated on T01 completion | `assets/t01-network-map-v1.json` |

Participant-facing instructions are the [team
workflow](../participants/cells.md) and the [beginner
guide](../expanded/guides.md); this document describes what those instructions
are meant to produce.

## The framework mapping, and why it is not verified

The current framework is **NICE Framework 4.0**, published in **NIST SP 800-160
Rev. 2**, restructured around TLP elements: Task, Knowledge and Skill.

SP 800-181 Rev. 1 is superseded. The Planning Note that accompanies NIST SP
800-181 Rev. 1 records that the Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity is now
maintained as NICE Framework 4.0 in SP 800-160 Rev. 2. That supersession is the
one framework fact this repository can state as verified.

Every four-digit task identifier and every `PD-WRL-*` work role identifier
below is carried as **unverified candidate** text from the superseded 2.2.0
listing. None has been checked against the 4.0 catalogue, because that
catalogue was not reachable when this document was generated. They are printed
so a reviewer can adjudicate them, not because they are asserted: 4.0
reorganised tasks around TLP elements, so an identifier that was correct in
2.2.0 may be renumbered, absorbed or withdrawn.

The previous revision of this document asserted that task IDs are stable across
the NICE revision, with no citation. That assertion is withdrawn: a
restructuring around TLP elements makes stability implausible and nothing in
this repository evidences it. Candidate entries naming a capability the
exercise states it does not demonstrate - forensic duplication, notification,
containment - were removed rather than carried, so the mapping does not assert
what the run cannot show.

| Publication | Status in this document |
|---|---|
| NICE Framework 4.0 (NIST SP 800-160 Rev. 2) | current base publication |
| NIST SP 800-181 Rev. 1 / NICE Framework Components version 2.2.0, with the 2.0-era role identifiers `PR-CDA-001` and `PR-CIR-001` | superseded; recorded as provenance only |
| `framework.verified_against` | null |

**Gate.** `verified: false`. 32 of 32 candidate mappings (26 distinct
identifiers) are unverified. framework.verified_against is null, so no mapping
may be called verified; set it to the dated NICE release the identifiers were
checked against.

## Investigation phases, and an open partition decision

The exercise is delivered in four investigation phases. `ridge/narrative.py`
feeds a phase, a briefing, a stake and a handoff into every authored ticket, so
each ticket arrives with its context rather than as a bare prompt.

**Two fixtures in the tree partition the twenty tickets differently, and this
document does not assert either partition as fact.** Naming one as *the* phase
layout would be a claim this repository cannot support until the conflict is
decided.

The decision is open in PR #151, which is the same pull request that carries
the contract, the deck, the map and the ten cross-surface guards. Until it
lands, a ticket's phase is a property of the surface being read, not of the
exercise.

What a reader can rely on today is the unlock graph in `expanded/author.py`:
prerequisites, not phases, decide what a team can work and in what order.

| Fixture | Read by | Phase ids | Tickets per phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| `assets/scenario-narrative-v1.json` | ridge/scenario_contract.py | phase-1, phase-2, phase-3, phase-4 | 3 / 8 / 5 / 4 |
| `ridge/scenario_narrative_v1.json` | ridge/narrative.py | disclosure, identity, scope, assessment | 5 / 5 / 5 / 5 |

The two partitions assign a different phase to 20 of the 20 tickets.

## Tool and view semantics

Two Wazuh data views are provisioned for this exercise and the authored steps
select between them. The previous revision of this document told participants
to use one `silent-ridge-*` view with an absolute UTC range for every Wazuh
ticket, which cannot produce the coverage ticket's answers: its own step is
overridden to use a view without a time field.

A coverage or catalogue record describes a collection interval rather than an
event, so it carries no event timestamp and a time picker cannot select it.
`ridge/scenario.py` encodes the same distinction in `TIMELESS_SOURCES`.

This is the defect `ridge/learning_objectives.py` now refuses to let back in:
the documented view partition is derived from the authored ticket steps, so
merging the two views fails validation.

| Tickets | Saved view | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `T06`, `T07`, `T10`, `T11`, `T20` | `silent-ridge-timed` | dated event and inventory records; absolute scenario-date UTC range |
| `T12` | `silent-ridge-timeless` | coverage records carry no event timestamp, so the time picker hides them |

## Clock semantics and the two dates

`ridge/scenario.py` subtracts the documented device offset from a `device_time`
field and from no other field. Proxy and DNS rows carry an already-normalized
`time`, and the telemetry loader normalizes to UTC once.

Apply a correction only where the source gives an offset, and never re-correct
a record that is already normalized. `expanded/guides.md` states the same rule
to participants.

The two dates are a month apart on purpose, and the divergence is the lesson.
The historical incident is dated 2026-10-15. The native Windows reconstruction
recorded in assets/native-windows-v1/manifest.json was acquired 2026-09-15, and
its records carry actual
acquisition UTC rather than historical incident time. A team that applies the
historical offset to the native records has joined two evidence systems and two
clocks, which is the error those two tickets exist to catch.

| Fact | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Device offset | WS-17 is 120 seconds fast | `ridge/scenario.py` `DEVICE_OFFSETS` |
| Tickets that apply the correction | `T04` | their questions ask for a corrected time |
| Tickets that ask for the offset itself | `T12` | the coverage record states the drift |
| Tickets that must not be corrected | `T13`, `T14`, `T15`, `T16` | native records; one of them answers that question with `no` |
| Scenario date | 2026-10-15 | `expanded/config.json` |
| Native acquisition date | 2026-09-15 | `assets/native-windows-v1/manifest.json` |

## The T01 exfiltration network map

`assets/t01-network-map-v1.json` renders as one self-contained offline view of
the reconstructed outbound path. It is an additional analytical view, not a
second source of truth: it replaces no question, adds none and scores nothing.

It is deliberately **not** a released evidence file. Transport publishes a
ticket's release files when that ticket unlocks, and T01 unlocks at run start,
so a released map would have named the destination before the ticket that
scores it was answered. It is served from the question page and gated on the
same condition that closes T01. `ridge/network_map.py` records the reasoning.

Every edge carries `observed` or `inferred`. An observed edge is stated in full
by one published record; an inferred edge joins two or more records and names
what it joins and what it does not show. Records are joined on request, path
and normalized UTC time, never on the rewritten id column.

Counts read from `assets/t01-network-map-v1.json`: 19 nodes, 13 edges, 11
observed in a single record and 2 inferred by joining records.

## Objectives

Nine objectives, each stated as something a participant can do rather than a
topic they have been exposed to, each naming the tickets that score it and the
mechanism in the exercise that produces it. A ticket may be claimed by more
than one objective where the same investigation genuinely serves two
capabilities; `validate` refuses the document while any ticket is claimed by
none.

The ordering below is deliberate on two points. Provenance and clock semantics
sit before chain-building, because a join made across two clocks is not a join.
And the observed-versus-inferred discipline has an objective of its own,
because the repository enforces it hardest in code:
`ridge/scenario_contract.py`, `ridge/network_map.py` and every authored
finding's `limitation` all exist to keep a claim inside what a record states.

### LO1 - State where every timestamp came from

Name the source and the clock convention behind every time quoted, apply a
correction only where the source gives one, and never re-correct a record that
is already normalized or already dated by an acquisition.

**Tickets.** `T03`, `T04`, `T12`, `T13`, `T14` (5 of 20).

**Mechanism.** Only `T04` applies the documented 120-second WS-17 device
correction, because the offset is subtracted from a `device_time` field and
from nothing else; `T12` asks the offset's value and is read in the view
without a time field, so a second correction there is visibly wrong. `T13` and
`T14` are a different evidence system on a different day: the native
reconstruction acquired 2026-09-15, whose manifest records actual acquisition
UTC, and `T14` scores `no` for applying the historical offset to it. `T03`
supplies the already-normalized browser record the corrected endpoint time is
reconciled against.

**Achievement evidence.** Times quoted with their source and convention, the
offset applied exactly once to the one field that carries a device clock, and
an answer that keeps the acquisition clock distinct from the scenario clock.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1250` Perform incident triage |
| Digital Forensics `PD-WRL-002` | `T0168` Perform data comparison against established database |

### LO2 - Build the chain only where records share an identifier

Join two records only where they share an identifier, and say which identifier
does the joining. A causal story held together by plausibility is not a chain.

**Tickets.** `T01`, `T02`, `T03`, `T05`, `T13`, `T14`, `T15`, `T16`, `T19` (9
of 20).

**Mechanism.** One request identifier links the plan download on the wire to
the server access record and a second links the outbound upload to the
transmitted body; a resolved name links the lookup to the address; a session
identifier spans identity, endpoint and server records; a content hash links
the transmitted body to the service catalogue. `T15` is the join the exercise
needs most: the recovered cache file name and the cache argument recorded in
the running process are the same string, so a deleted file and a live process
corroborate each other instead of merely repeating. `T16` then carries the same
process identifier across the acquired process, memory and connection records.

**Achievement evidence.** Answers that name the joining identifier rather than
the resemblance, and at least one place where two records were *not* joined
because nothing identified them as the same thing.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1391` Reconstruct malicious attacks; `T1348` Distinguish between benign and potentially malicious attacks and intrusions |
| Incident Response `PD-WRL-003` | `T1489` Correlate incident data; `T1252` Determine the scope, urgency, and impact of cyber defense incidents |

### LO3 - Keep the evidence defensible

Work from a copy, treat the released source and the untouched original as two
different objects, and verify the link between them before you rely on a value.

**Tickets.** `T05`, `T13`, `T14`, `T17` (4 of 20).

**Mechanism.** There are two read-only mounts, not one: released sources under
`/evidence` and the untouched originals under `/originals`. The Autopsy tickets
open a writable copy of the prepared case on the team desktop while both mounts
stay read-only, and the prepared native records carry `original_path` and
`original_sha256`, so the prepared view can be checked against the original it
was derived from. `T05` recovers a deleted cache entry by searching a surviving
filename suffix rather than assuming its contents. The Cutter training binary
is a real artifact gated on a hash and is inspected statically, never executed.
Imaging, live containment, agent installation and large ingest jobs are out of
scope during the exercise.

**Achievement evidence.** A finding whose value traces to a released source,
and where a native record is used, to the original hash it names; the writable
case used for work and nothing written to either mount; the deleted entry
recovered rather than assumed.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Digital Forensics `PD-WRL-002` | `T1510` Preserve digital evidence; `T1199` Identify digital evidence for analysis |

### LO4 - Judge whether the credential action contained the incident

Separate the two authentication events, read the multi-factor semantics of the
session, and decide from the supplied policy whether the credential action
actually ended the session.

**Tickets.** `T06`, `T07` (2 of 20).

**Mechanism.** `T06` uses the Wazuh replay to separate the external session
refresh from the failed password login, and to read the refresh's multi-factor
field rather than assuming a fresh challenge was performed. `T07` then tests
what the password reset actually did, against the later successful refresh and
the supplied identity policy, and unlocks only after `T06` - so a team cannot
conclude that the incident was contained without first having separated the two
events.

**Achievement evidence.** A session-centric answer that concludes the reset was
insufficient without explicit revocation, that cites the later refresh rather
than the reset time, and that treats an address as non-attributive.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Incident Response `PD-WRL-003` | `T1250` Perform incident triage |
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1548` Determine adequacy of access controls |
| Insider Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-005` | `T1324` Process digital evidence |

### LO5 - Bound the disclosure

Quantify what left using response codes, byte counts, object versions and a
content comparison, and keep disclosed objects separate from denied ones.

**Tickets.** `T08`, `T09`, `T19` (3 of 20).

**Mechanism.** `T08` separates a successful download from a denied request by
status code and body-byte count, which is the difference between a disclosed
object and an attempted one. `T09` compares a superseding version against the
earlier one; a superseding version changes what should have been sent, not what
was already sent, so the comparison is bounded to what each version states.
`T19` matches the transmitted body hash against the service catalogue, which is
what identifies *which* version was transmitted. Each authored finding records
its own limitation.

**Achievement evidence.** A scope position that names the single disclosed
object and its version, names the denied request as a denial rather than a
disclosure, and states the collection limits the comparison rests on.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1351` Determine impact of malicious activity; `T1548` Determine adequacy of access controls |
| Incident Response `PD-WRL-003` | `T1252` Determine the scope, urgency, and impact of cyber defense incidents |
| Vulnerability Analysis `PD-WRL-007` | `T1020` Determine the operational and safety impacts of cybersecurity lapses |

### LO6 - Keep an unresolved lead open

Clear a benign comparator before calling something suspicious, then hold a
per-host scope position open where the collection cannot support a conclusion.
Absence of telemetry is not absence of activity.

**Tickets.** `T10`, `T11`, `T12` (3 of 20).

**Mechanism.** `T10` establishes an approved, similarly named scheduled task on
another host and is a result in its own right: clearing a host is worth more
than another suspicious finding. `T11` then finds the same tool name on a host
whose endpoint collection stopped mid-morning, and it unlocks only after `T10`,
so a team cannot reach the unresolved lead without first having cleared the
benign one. That ordering is pedagogical, not accidental. `T12` supplies the
coverage record that explains the lead, and is read in the view without a time
field because a collection interval is not an event.

**Achievement evidence.** A per-host position of supported, suspected, benign
or unobservable in which the unobservable host stays unobservable, a
reproducible filter per hypothesis, and no enterprise-wide all-clear derived
from a collection gap.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-006` | `T1053` Identify and characterize intrusion activities; `T1054` Scope analysis reports to audiences |
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1084` Identify anomalous network activity; `T1350` Perform continuous monitoring of system activity |
| Insider Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-005` | `T1743` Identify information collection gaps |

### LO7 - Label a statement observed or inferred, and say what it does not establish

Mark every relationship you assert as observed in one record or inferred by
joining several, and state what the relationship does not prove.

**Tickets.** `T01`, `T02`, `T16`, `T17`, `T18` (5 of 20).

**Mechanism.** Every authored finding carries a limitation, and several
questions are scored directly on it. The T01 map makes the distinction visible
rather than verbal: it is gated behind T01 completion precisely so it cannot
pre-answer the ticket, and each of its edges declares its own basis and caveat.
`T16` is the sharpest case: it is an acquired live connection snapshot and not
a validated memory connection finding, and its own record shows the external
address was a guest-local loopback in an isolated reconstruction with
networking disabled - so an over-stated conclusion about it is demonstrably
wrong from the record itself. `T17` and `T18` show that configuration present
in a file is not execution of that configuration.

**Achievement evidence.** Every asserted relationship labelled observed or
inferred, every inference naming what it joins, and at least one explicit
statement of what the evidence does not establish - receipt, reading, intent or
attribution.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Digital Forensics `PD-WRL-002` | `T1324` Process digital evidence; `T0167` Perform file signature analysis; `T1607` Recover information from forensic data sources |
| Defensive Cybersecurity `PD-WRL-001` | `T1386` Analyze network traffic anomalies |

### LO8 - State the boundary of the exposure

Conclude what the evidence supports and name what it does not support, in the
same answer and without waiting to be asked twice.

**Tickets.** `T20` (1 of 20).

**Mechanism.** `T20` unlocks only after the identity, version, lead and payload
tickets, so the boundary cannot be stated without that work behind it. **Three
of its four answers are `no`**, and that is the thesis of the exercise rather
than an oversight: roster disclosure is not established by a denied request,
the unresolved host cannot be cleared with the available telemetry, and the
evidence does not establish adversary intent. A correct boundary is a result,
not a failure to find one. There is deliberately no adversary name anywhere in
the corpus, and the exercise has no notification path and no manager to notify.

**Achievement evidence.** A closing conclusion that names the one supported
exposure, leaves the three unknowns open with the reason each cannot be closed,
and attributes the activity to no one.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Incident Response `PD-WRL-003` | `T1316` Document incidents; `T1252` Determine the scope, urgency, and impact of cyber defense incidents |
| Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-006` | `T1054` Scope analysis reports to audiences |

### LO9 - Publish durable shared findings and run the after-action review

Publish each accepted answer as a finding other teams can use, continue another
team's work without losing it, and turn the run into specific improvements.

**Tickets.** `T07`, `T09`, `T19`, `T20` (4 of 20).

**Mechanism.** A correct answer queues an authored finding to IRIS and an award
to CTFd through durable outbox retries and application-side receipts, so an
accepted finding is not duplicated across an outage and is not lost to one.
Relinquishing a ticket keeps its answers and findings for the replacement
owner. The dependency chain is what makes the shared findings usable: `T20` is
answered from findings other teams produced, on tickets they unlocked. The
[after-action review](../facilitator/assessment-aar.md) is the reflection
mechanism, and there is no report, grading or approval gate anywhere in the
run.

**Achievement evidence.** A follow-up ticket answered from another team's
finding, continued progress after a relinquish or a service interruption, and
improvement items from the review carrying an owner, a target rehearsal date
and an observable success criterion.

| Work role (candidate) | Candidate tasks (unverified) |
|---|---|
| Incident Response `PD-WRL-003` | `T0510` Coordinate incident response functions; `T1485` Prepare after action reviews; `T1333` Communicate incident findings |
| Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-006` | `T1643` Develop common operational pictures |
| Insider Threat Analysis `PD-WRL-005` | `T1986` Develop a continuously updated overview of an incident throughout its life cycle |

## Duration

The exercise has 20 tickets and 80 scored questions. Authored estimates total
1300 team-minutes, about 130.0 minutes per team for 10 teams, and the simulated
makespan is 195 minutes on the critical path T06 -> T07 -> T20. The configured
activity target is 270 minutes.

The per-team figure is a quotient, not a plan: ten teams share one global owner
per ticket, and the dependency chain with the limited number of initially
available tickets is what sets the makespan.

The previous revision of this document called the target a four-hour goal and
omitted the makespan. The configured target is 270 minutes, the midpoint of the
event owner's confirmed 240-300 minute activity window (decided 2026-09-17),
and the modelled makespan is 195 minutes.

Free walkthroughs reduce unaided work below the estimate, so the authored
content covers roughly half the target window. Closing that gap means more
authored content or facilitated segments around the investigations, not
duplicated scoreable tickets per team.

Every figure here is planning arithmetic from `expanded/author.py`, not a
measurement. Only a beginner rehearsal, recorded on the [rehearsal
worksheet](rehearsal-worksheet.md), can replace it; the current numbers are in
the [workload inventory](workload.md).

## How the after-action review revisits the objectives

There is no rubric. `facilitator/assessment-aar.md` uses the scoreboard and the
shared IRIS findings for discussion, and each prompt exercises one or more
objectives.

| AAR prompt | Objectives most exercised |
|---|---|
| How clock normalization or a cross-source correlation changed an assessment | LO1, LO2 |
| What versions, sessions, denied accesses and collection gaps establish | LO2, LO4, LO5 |
| Which uncertainties remain and what further evidence would resolve them | LO5, LO6 |
| Where a finding claimed more than its evidence supported | LO7, LO8 |
| Whether shared findings and ownership transfers helped other teams | LO8, LO9 |
| Which tool instructions or exercise defects need improvement before the next run | LO1, LO3, LO7 |

## Out of scope and current limits

- Defensive and synthetic. The exercise teaches and assesses defensive analysis
  only. It does not teach offensive access, malware reverse engineering or live
  imaging, and the Cutter binary is a harmless training surrogate that performs
  no network or persistence behaviour.

- No forensic duplication is demonstrated. Participants read supplied read-only
  originals and work in a copy of a prepared case. That is coached practice,
  not assessed mastery of acquiring a forensic duplicate: no scored item claims
  the skill, and no objective above maps to one. The Cutter binary is a real
  artifact gated on a hash, and it is inspected statically rather than
  executed.

- Artifacts exist; whole-event acceptance does not. The native Windows
  reconstruction (`assets/native-windows-v1/manifest.json`), the prepared
  Autopsy case (`assets/autopsy-case-v2.json`) and the offline desktop image
  (`assets/desktop-v1.json`) are published and checksummed, so the
  acquired-record tickets have prepared artifacts to reference. That is not a
  validated deployment: per `docs/expanded-validation.md`, no question has yet
  been navigated and answered on the exact installed tools, and Hyper-V and AWS
  boot, Guacamole sessions and live IRIS and CTFd behaviour remain unverified.

- The exercise is not event-ready. No Docker, CTFd, IRIS, Wazuh or desktop
  container has been run against these guards. They are proven to fire, not
  proven readable to a person. Do not read a passing test suite as a rehearsal
  result, and do not describe this material as live-validated.

- The projected deck is behind its sources. The event-day deck is 22
  participant slides plus a 2-slide facilitator appendix, and the committed PDF
  is still the earlier 13-slide build because the external toolchain that
  renders it is not vendored here. The `.page` sources are authoritative and
  the PDF must be rebuilt before the deck is projected; `python -m
  ridge.deck_narrative --pdf` reports the staleness rather than pretending
  otherwise.

- Breadcrumbs are optional and unscored, deliberately. Seven breadcrumbs are
  left in the evidence, five of them cross-task. None is bonus-scored: stock
  CTFd challenges are locked down in this deployment, scoring is one award row
  per answered question, and no surface exists that could carry a bonus and
  reconcile it against both systems. A team that finds none has done the
  exercise correctly.

- The framework mapping is unverified. Every identifier in the tables above is
  a candidate carried from a superseded release. See the framework section for
  the gate, and re-verify against a dated catalogue release before claiming any
  formal mapping for training credit.

## Maintenance

Edit `assets/learning-objectives-v1.json`, then run `python -m
ridge.learning_objectives --write` and commit both. `python -m
ridge.learning_objectives` validates without writing, `--report` prints the
receipt, and `--strict` additionally fails while the NICE gate is open. A test
compares the committed document with `render()` byte for byte, so a hand edit
to the document fails the suite rather than shipping.

Validation derives the ticket set and every ticket title from
`expanded/author.py`, the saved view names from `ridge/wazuh_provision.py`, the
device offset from `ridge/scenario.py`, the acquisition date from the native
manifest, the map counts from `assets/t01-network-map-v1.json`, the phase
partitions from both narrative fixtures, the duration figures from
`expanded/config.json` through `expanded/workload.py`, and the answer set from
the same authored questions. Changing any of those changes what this document
is required to say. When a ticket is added, retitled or reassigned, update the
fixture and the crosswalk in the same commit; when an objective is added,
`validate` refuses until every ticket is claimed.

Do not add, renumber or "correct" a NICE identifier from memory. Re-verify each
mapping against a dated published catalogue, record that release in
`framework.verified_against`, and note in the pull request that NICE Framework
4.0 reorganised tasks around TLP elements, so a 2.0-era identifier may not
survive the mapping unchanged.
